title: At the Service Court
notes: An optional conversation at the service court. The visible outlines are an unstable human trace, not a body or speaking identity for HUSH. Movement cues on the lines (hush-pose.js) belong to that trace; HUSH remains nonverbal pressure in the space. The recordist's own faculties speak around it — METER, TAPE, HANDS, EARS, and the recordist (you/me). Two menus: ask (questions) and examine (things you do). Talk two opens the case of the recordist before you (dock clues and papers unlock questions); talk three asks what it agreed to. The warning is an argument between the voices that have earned a side. Checks read what the night already gave you (takes, composure, patch leads) and never gate the fight; one-shot checks are gone once tried. A few actions leave small tells for the Source fight. The warning is available on the first meeting; no conversation count, answer or tour qualifies it. Only the explicit warned confirmation starts battle. Leaving never relocates the player or closes the route back.

lines.text: A human outline waits at the service court, a few paces away. The way past it is open.
No footsteps. You did not hear it arrive.
-18 on the needle, and steady. Nothing in this court is making a sound.
You can hear me.
Your hands have come away from your sides, palms out. Nobody told them to.
It turns before you speak. The hand is still open.
It does not turn this time. It was already facing the way you would come.
Same court, take two. On a job you would slate it that way and pretend the first one never happened.
Your body has stopped treating it like a stranger. That is not the same as trusting it.
The carrier is still in your ear. The breath on the set had exactly this shape.
-18 again. It picks the level up where it left it.
Your weight has gone to the back foot by itself. You stood like that for it once already.
The thin source is still there, low down, just behind it.
Your hand has started toward it before you have decided anything. You have to tell it to wait.

choices.text: Ask the one on the floor if it is hurt.
Ask about the recordist who came before you.

lines.text: Its head tilts. A second outline lags behind the first: a shoulder, a sleeve, a hand held in the same position.
Someone is still in there.
The hand closes. For a moment, only the smaller outline moves.
Two voices on one reel sound like that. Not an echo. A second take, laid over the first before the first was wiped.
You. Not the tall one. You.
Neither outline answers. The larger steps half across the smaller, the way you would stand in front of a child at a door.
Your hand has come up flat, the gesture for all right, all right. You didn't send it.
It's protecting it. Or it's keeping it.
It looks at the recorder. The level meter rises although neither of you has made a sound.
-31. -24. -19. Climbing, on a room that isn't getting any louder.
Not me. What I brought with me.
You cover the microphone with your palm. The level does not fall.
Still -19. Whatever it's reading, it isn't coming in through the capsule.

choices.text: Unhook the recorder. Hold it out to it.
Put the recorder back on your shoulder. Ask something else.

lines.text: You unhook the strap and hold the machine out at arm's length, reels toward it.
Every room you've finished tonight is on that spool. It isn't looking at you. It's looking at the spool.
It leans in. Not toward you. Toward the reels.
It wants what's on the tape. Or it wants to be on it.
You hold the machine out. The window shows clean leader on both reels.
Nothing on it yet. Not one room. You've brought it an empty tape.
It doesn't move. There is nothing on the machine for it to want.
It turns toward the open ground, leaving enough room for you to pass.
The court comes back wrong. Too short a tail on your breath, as if there's a wall two metres out that you can't see.
I can go on. I don't have to do this.
It does not follow your glance. It is still watching the hand nearest the recorder.
I'm the one doing the fifth room.
The smaller outline lifts its head. The larger one doesn't let it get far.
Four slates on the reel before yours. Same voice, same breath before each number. He never got to say five.
You never got to say five.
The one on the floor. Are you hurt?
The larger outline turns its back on you, completely, for the first time, and stands over the place the thin sound was.
The thin source stops. Not gone. Held.
That's an answer. I just don't know what to.
You're a bad take. Noise on the reel. That's all you are.
Nothing changes. Then the needle drops to the stop, the way it does when somebody pulls a cable.
Minus infinity. Not quiet. Disconnected.
Your thumb is already on the input jack, pressing it home. It's seated.
The level comes back when you stop saying it.
Point taken.
Up close the edges don't hold. It is printed, not lit. The paper shows through where the shoulders should be.
Your pulse is in your thumbs. Keep them off the transport keys.

choices.text: Hold the microphone out. Say nothing.
Close your eyes. Listen for where it is.
"You're a bad take. That's all you are."

lines.text: You bring the beam up. The source behind it takes the light. At the shoulders, a thin second edge arrives a moment later.
Inside the pale shape there are two. One is the height of a man. One is shorter, and holds its arm the way you are holding the torch.
It's copying me. The small one's copying me.
Afterimage. When the beam drops, the small one stays burned in a second longer. Remember which is which.
You hold the microphone out at arm's length, the way you would to a stranger in the street.
Rising. Not from sound. From distance closing, and it isn't its distance. It's yours.
You haven't moved. You look down to be sure.
'Room five, take one.' That's the slate that belongs here. Nobody has said it.
I didn't say anything.
You set your weight on the back foot and let your right hand hang open, a little out from the hip.
It's wrong for a body. Held for long it would cramp. You hold it.
For a second there are two of you in the court. Then it shifts first: the smaller outline flinches, as if you had raised your voice.
It didn't like being matched. The small one didn't.
You try to stand the way it stands. Your knee won't lock.
Shaking. Too much of the night in your legs to hold a shape that isn't yours.
It watches you give up. Its hand doesn't move.
You close your eyes. The field hisses. Somewhere, paper is turned.
There. Two sources, not one. A low one a pace ahead of you, and a thin one just behind it, close to the floor, like someone sitting down.
Something's sitting down in there.
Hiss. Your own blood. The field. Nothing you can place. It's everywhere or it's nowhere.
When you open your eyes it is half a pace closer.
There is no floor under it. The printed lines on the paper run straight through where its feet should be, unbroken.
That's why there were no footsteps.
You say it plainly: the one before me. The larger outline goes still in a way that is not the same as not moving.
Four slates on his reel. Short, dry, close. A voice that didn't waste breath on the take number.

choices.text: "Four marks under the handle of your case."
"The last line on your work order. The chandelier."
"You wrote that it wanted a minute of you on the tape."
Ask if it heard the room before the slate.
Leave him out of it. Ask something else.

lines.text: Four marks under the handle of your case. Cut with a key. Room for a fifth.
The smaller outline's hand goes to its own hip, where a key would hang, and finds nothing.
Four rooms, four clean minutes. He kept count on the case, so the case would remember if he didn't.
You were going to cut the fifth when you came back up.
I snapped your latch on the dock. I know how it sounds.
And there it is. One small metal cough, from nowhere in the court. Exactly the pitch.
Neither outline moved. The sound came anyway.
It keeps his sounds. It keeps them where it can reach them.
The last line on your work order. Chandelier, frame and lock. You didn't tick it.
The larger outline lifts its head toward a ceiling that isn't there.
-40 and falling. Everything in the court just got quieter to listen.
You stopped at the chandelier. Or it stopped you.
Your notes. You wrote that it wanted a minute of you on the tape. That's all.
The smaller outline turns to the larger one, the way you turn to someone who has just been quoted.
'I was not sad, and I was not haunted.' His hand, sheet ten. 'It asked.'
You gave it the minute. And it kept the rest.
What did the client promise you?
The carbon says it. Names and consent at the gate, and the officer's field blank under every layer. Nobody living signed for this.
The larger outline opens its hand again, palm up, the way a contract is offered across a desk.
Nobody promised you anything. There wasn't anybody to promise.
What did the client promise you?
The hand stays open. Whatever it is offering, you don't have the paper to read it by.
Nothing on file. You never saw his copy of the order. You only have yours.
Before each of his slates there's a breath that isn't his. A second and a bit early. The room answering a question he hadn't asked yet.
The smaller outline flinches at the word early.
It was on your tape before you were.
Hiss before the slate. Just hiss. If there was anything there, you'd need better ears, or a better night.
The larger outline waits, as if you had missed something obvious.
You don't lower your voice. There is nobody here to lower it for.
Your hands have gone into your pockets. They do that when you're about to ask somebody to sign.

choices.text: "If I give it a minute of me, does he go free?"
Ask the one on the floor if it is hurt.

lines.text: Did you agree to this? Any of it?
The larger outline nods. Once, slowly, all the way down.
The smaller one doesn't. Its head stays where it is, and the two outlines come apart by a hand's width.
One of you agreed.
Whose body is that?
You ask it steadily. Your hands stay out of it.
The larger outline looks down at itself, at the arms, the way you look at a coat you've been lent.
A lent coat sits wrong at the shoulders. So does that.
It's his. It's wearing him.
Whose—
Your voice goes before the question does. Too much of the night in your throat.
It takes a step toward you, into the space where the end of the sentence should have been.
Not now. I can't ask that now.
The small one. Is that you?
The smaller outline raises its hand. Not to you. To the larger one's wrist, and holds it.
Two breaths, one held. The held one is the thin one.
You're still in there. And you're holding on.
Were you a student here? Before the files?
The needle jumps to the first bar of something and drops back. Rehearsal level. A room full of people correcting each other.
The larger outline flinches, the way a player does when somebody stops the tape mid-bar.
Not him. The thing wearing him learned here.
If I give it a minute of me on the tape, does he go free?
Nothing moves for so long that you check the meter.
-18. It was listening. It's still listening.
Your thumb has found the record key. It's resting on it. Take it off.
That's not a no.
Can he come back?
Sheet ten again: 'It asked.' Asked means there was someone to answer. Someone to answer is someone to return.
The smaller outline steps half out of the larger. For a moment there is air between them.
Then the larger closes the gap, gently, the way you would take back something you had only lent.
He can. It won't let him.
Can he come back?
Nothing. Not a lean, not a flinch. The question goes out across the court and does not come back.
You don't know enough about what was taken to ask for it back.
Before your fingers touch it, the smaller body recoils. The other holds its hand out. You can still lower yours.
Your hand wants to go. The rest of you is asking it to wait.
Room five. He never slated it. Maybe this is how it gets slated.
The thin one is breathing faster.
The needle's already against the stop, and you haven't touched it yet.
He gave it a minute. This will take a great deal more than a minute.
The small one isn't recoiling from you. It's pulling back from the other one's grip.
You're not steady enough for this, and every part of you that holds things knows it.
If he can come back, this is the only way I've found to ask for him.
If I touch it, I will have to fight it. I won't be able to retreat. If I lose, I die here.
You lower your hand and step back. It lets you.
-18. The needle settles where it found it.
You close the distance. Its fingers close around yours. The level meter strikes the end stop.
Not Martin. I'm not calling Martin.
No desk answers. The carrier opens anyway, and the hiss takes the shape of a wide room with one thing standing in it.
You can hear me on this too.
When you let go of the key, the breath in the speaker is not yours. It holds, the way a hand stays open.
